title: The fourth sight: a wanderer
hook: a shaven man in a robe, owning nothing, calm
carry: there is another way to live

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third sight: a funeral on the road, and the prince going quiet. Your line was everyone we love will go. Who did you call or message? Day thirty-four.
screen: `THE THIRD SIGHT — EVERYONE WE LOVE WILL GO.`

segments.voice: Three rides, three shocks. Age, sickness, death. If the story stopped there, it would be a very sad story, and the prince might have spent the rest of his life hiding in his gardens. But there's a fourth ride. Picture the prince now, more troubled than he has ever been, looking out from the chariot. And there, walking along the road, is a man with a shaved head, in a plain robe the color of earth. He carries a bowl. He owns, as far as anyone can tell, nothing else. And his face is calm. Not cheerful, not grim. Calm, in a world that just showed the prince three reasons to despair. Today's word is what that man was.
screen: `THREE RIDES, THREE SHOCKS.` → `A SHAVED HEAD, A BOWL, A ROBE.` → `A CALM FACE.`

segments.voice: The prince asks: who is that? And Channa says, that's a samana. A wanderer, one who has gone forth. The word samana comes from a root that means to strive, to make an effort. In the Buddha's India there were many of them: men, and some women, who left home, gave up property and family life, and walked the roads looking for the answer to exactly the questions the prince had just been asking. Why do we age? Why do we suffer? Is there a way out? They lived on what people put in their bowls, slept in forests and caves, and argued with each other in the town squares. The samanas weren't one group. There were many teachers and many paths. The Jains, whose tradition is still alive today, came from this same world. So did the Buddha himself: for the rest of his life, outsiders would call him the samana Gotama. Here's the heart of the fourth sight. The first three were questions. The fourth was a possibility. The prince had just learned that age, sickness and death come for everyone, palace or no palace. And here was someone who had looked at the same facts and was not afraid. The stories say something in the prince went still and bright. Not an answer yet. Just the sense that there is another way to live, and that someone, somewhere, is already living it. That sense, that another way exists, is where every search begins.
screen: `SAMANA — ONE WHO STRIVES.` · `MANY WANDERERS, MANY PATHS.` · `THREE QUESTIONS, ONE POSSIBILITY.` · `SOMEONE ALREADY LIVES IT.` · then, large: `THERE IS ANOTHER WAY TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath find its own rhythm. Bring to mind the calmest face you have ever seen. It might be someone you know, a teacher, a grandparent, a stranger on a train, even a statue. Hold the face in your mind. Notice what calm looks like: the eyes, the mouth, the shoulders. Now, gently, let your own face do a little of the same. Soften the jaw. Let the eyes rest. You're not pretending. You're just letting calm be possible for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Samana. A wanderer, one who strives: someone who has left home to seek the truth. The fourth sight, and the first hope.
Your line: there is another way to live. Today, find one calm face, at work, on the street, on a screen, and let it remind you that calm is possible. Day thirty-four.

howItsDone: Buddhist monks and nuns today still follow the samana's way of life in many places, shaving their heads, wearing robes and receiving food as alms, and lay Buddhists often honor them as living examples of another way to live.

fork.setup: you've just seen age, sickness and death, and now a calm man with a bowl walks by. what do you ask?
fork.reveal: he asks who the man is. Channa tells him: a samana, one who has gone forth. and something in the prince goes still and bright.

original.note: Pali: a wanderer, an ascetic, one who strives. Sanskrit śramaṇa.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monk the prince happened to see.
what it means: after three sights of suffering, the fourth shows someone at peace with the same facts. it's the first hope in the story.
what a scholar hears: samana (Sanskrit śramaṇa), from a root meaning to exert oneself; the samana movements, including Jains and Ajivikas, stood outside the brahmin priesthood.

sources.ref: Mahapadana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 14): the one gone forth, the fourth sight
Samannaphala Sutta (Digha Nikaya 2): the wandering teachers of the Buddha's time

notes: Etymology of samana/śramaṇa from the root śram, to exert oneself; confirm.
'Some women' among the wanderers: women ascetics (e.g., among the Jains) are attested; confirm the phrasing is fair for the period.
'The samana Gotama' as outsiders' name for the Buddha: common in the suttas (samano Gotamo). Confirm.
The prince's inner response to the fourth sight is from the later biographies; DN 14 has Vipassi decide to go forth. Confirm the framing.
